extracted.intended_audience: students and scholars of poetics and literary criticism; poets and dramatists
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance for evaluating and composing poetry/drama according to Aristotle's Poetics, emphasising universality, internal probability/necessity, treatment of the marvellous, character-motive coherence, avoidance of chance, and organic unity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Poetry expresses the universal (not the particular)
rubrics_metrics.description: “Poetry expresses most adequately the universal element in human nature and in life... It is not the function of the poet to relate what has happened, but what may happen.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Poetry abstracts from the accidental and particular; it liberates thought from sense and material needs and transforms factual material into universal truths. The poet's subject-matter is the permanent possibilities of human nature rather than particular historical events.

rubrics_metrics.name: Internal causal connexion / rule of probability or necessity
rubrics_metrics.description: “Poetry exhibits a more rigorous connexion of events; cause and event are linked together in ‘probable or necessary sequence’.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The rule of probability/necessity governs the internal structure of a poem or drama: events must follow by intelligible causal or probable links rather than merely chronological succession. ‘Probability’ here is not statistical vraisemblance to everyday life but coherence within the poem’s own law.

rubrics_metrics.name: Characters must act with moral and logical coherence
rubrics_metrics.description: “In the internal working of character, the drama observes a stricter and more logical order than that of actual experience.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Character behaviour must be intelligible and motivated; moral improbabilities (motiveless or unintelligible actions) are serious defects. The chain of causes in drama is formed by human will meeting outward circumstances; violations of character-consistency (e.g., motiveless ignorance or sudden inexplicable acts) break the plot's unity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Distinguish essential poetic errors from errors of fact
rubrics_metrics.description: “He points out the distinction between errors affecting the essence of the poetic art, and errors of fact relating to other arts.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Minor factual oversights, inconsistencies, or technical inaccuracies are not in themselves fatal provided the total impression is unimpaired. Essential errors that affect the structure, unity, or moral logic of the work are the real defects to guard against.

rubrics_metrics.name: Poetic truth as a 'higher reality' — representing what ought to be
rubrics_metrics.description: “Not real, but a higher reality... what ought to be, not what is.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Poetry may transcend empirical fact to represent ideal forms or deeper truths. Such idealization is a legitimate aim of poetic art and can produce a truer understanding than mere factual reportage.

rubrics_metrics.name: Poet's licence to set primary fictional premises and preserve internal consistency
rubrics_metrics.description: “The poet must be allowed to make certain primary assumptions and create his own environment... Starting from these poetic data ... he may go whither he will, so long as he does not dash us against the prosaic ground of fact.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The poet can invent presuppositions and an imaginative environment; from these premises events must follow naturally. The strength of the illusion depends on vivid narrative, plausible sequence, and maintaining internal coherence (avoid the converse-fallacy of assuming consequents imply antecedents).

rubrics_metrics.name: Material impossibilities admissible if rendered plausible (probable impossibilities preferred)
rubrics_metrics.description: “The impossible not only becomes possible, but natural and even inevitable... ‘Probable impossibilities are to be preferred to improbable possibilities.’”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Materially impossible or marvellous incidents can be acceptable when the poet makes them appear inevitable within the poem’s logic (e.g., Homer’s handling of the Phaeacian ship or Odysseus’ landing). Vivid detail and coherent motive/sequence can transform impossibility into believable poetic event.

rubrics_metrics.name: Irrational elements require special justification and are riskier than material impossibilities
rubrics_metrics.description: “The ddoya... which the logical understanding rejects, are greater stumbling-blocks to the poetic sense than mere material impossibilities.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Irrational (logically incoherent or motiveless) elements provoke critical resistance and are harder to assimilate; they demand stronger justification (e.g., heightened wonder or tradition) and are more dangerous to dramatic effect than mere physical improbabilities.

rubrics_metrics.name: Heightened wonder/admirational effect can justify marvellous elements (especially in epic)
rubrics_metrics.description: “This justification Aristotle discovers in the heightened wonder and admiration, which he regards as proper, in a peculiar degree, to epic poetry.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Epic poetry may admit certain irrational or marvellous incidents when they provoke pleasurable astonishment that effaces incongruity. Some incidents (like Achilles’ chase of Hector) may be permissible in narrative epic though unsuitable on stage because the medium modulates their effect.

rubrics_metrics.name: Traditional/popular belief can justify marvellous or supernatural material
rubrics_metrics.description: “If not true, they are believed to be true... Current beliefs like these cannot be wholly ignored or rudely rejected by the poet... ‘yet so runs the tale.’”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Material rooted in long-standing mythology or national belief may be admissible because it is part of the audience's belief-system. Distinguish between legends that have been assimilated into coherent myth (admissible) and crude unassimilated irrational elements (problematic).

rubrics_metrics.name: Irrational/marvellous elements are more admissible in epic than in drama; drama demands motive
rubrics_metrics.description: “Aristotle holds that the irrational... is less admissible in dramatic than in epic poetry.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Drama is a typical representation of human action driven by motive; irrational or motiveless elements have no place within dramatic action (they might at most be part of antecedents), and if present should be treated sparingly and made plausible.

rubrics_metrics.name: Exclude chance/accident; prefer design and causal necessity
rubrics_metrics.description: “Chance... is the negation of Art and Intelligence... It is an irrational cause; it suggests anarchy and misrule; it has no proper place in poetry.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Poetry should avoid relying on accidental events or 'strange chances' to resolve plot; the law of the probable and of the necessary excludes unmotivated accidents except where the poet can convincingly make them appear designed. The principle undercuts the defence that ‘strange chances which occur in life’ justify implausible plot turns.

rubrics_metrics.name: Comedy must also observe probability; it is not a realm of pure chance
rubrics_metrics.description: “The incidents of comedy—at least of such comedy as Aristotle approves—are ‘framed on lines of probability.’”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Comedy's plot may be looser than tragedy's, but even comedic incidents should follow probable or plausible motives; comedy is not licence for random or chance-driven events that would violate artistic cohesion.

rubrics_metrics.name: Unity and wholeness: the plot as an organic whole
rubrics_metrics.description: “A unity is composed of a plurality of parts which cohere together... A whole... parts must be inwardly connected, arranged in a certain order, structurally related, and combined into a system.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A poetic work (especially tragedy) must be an organism: parts are structurally related and arranged to develop from within. Unity is not mere aggregation; the plot must unfold according to its own nature and produce a significant integrated whole.

rubrics_metrics.name: Appropriate magnitude/proportion of the work
rubrics_metrics.description: “If it is too small the whole is perceived but not the parts; if too large the parts are perceived but not the whole.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The size and extent of a work must be balanced so that both unity and plurality are perceived; magnitude should serve the form (analogy drawn to the proper size of a city, musical ensemble, or organism).
